reference.source: Youmans & Winn Neurological Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: Spondylolisthesis is forward (or occasionally backward) slippage of one vertebra on the one below, most often at the lumbosacral junction

Isthmic slips relate to a defect in the pars interarticularis (spondylolysis), often from repetitive extension stress in young athletes, while degenerative slips occur in older adults from facet and disc degeneration
Many slips are asymptomatic; when symptomatic, patients report low back pain, hamstring tightness, and sometimes radicular leg pain or neurogenic claudication
Severity is commonly graded by the degree of slip relative to the vertebral body width, which helps guide monitoring and management
Standing lateral and flexion-extension radiographs are useful to demonstrate the slip and any dynamic instability
Most cases are managed conservatively with activity modification, physiotherapy focusing on core stabilisation, and analgesia
Surgery, typically decompression with or without fusion, is considered for persistent disabling symptoms, neurological deficit, or progressive high-grade slips
High-grade slips in the skeletally immature warrant closer surveillance because of the potential for progression
reference.pathophysiology: Spondylolisthesis is displacement of one vertebra relative to the adjacent vertebra, usually anterior translation of the upper on the lower body. In isthmic disease a stress-related defect or fracture of the pars interarticularis (spondylolysis) allows the anterior elements to slip forward. In degenerative disease, age-related disc narrowing and facet joint arthropathy reduce the segment's stability and permit gradual slippage, typically without a pars defect. The malalignment can narrow the central canal and neural foramina, tethering or compressing nerve roots and, in higher grades, causing back pain and radicular or claudicant symptoms.
additionalInvestigations: Standing lateral radiographs to demonstrate and grade the slip
Flexion-extension views to assess dynamic instability
MRI to evaluate neural compression, disc, and root involvement
CT or oblique views to characterise a pars defect when suspected
Bone imaging (e.g. SPECT or MRI) in young athletes for a suspected active pars stress injury
redFlags: New or progressive neurological deficit or radiculopathy
Cauda equina symptoms such as saddle anaesthesia or sphincter disturbance
High-grade or progressive slip, particularly in a young or skeletally immature patient
Severe unremitting pain or features suggesting infection or malignancy
reference.prognosis: Most low-grade, degenerative, and isthmic slips remain stable and respond well to conservative care; higher-grade slips and those with neurological compromise are more likely to need surgery, which generally improves symptoms though progression can occur in growing patients.
pitfalls: Relying on supine imaging, which can underestimate a slip that is only apparent when standing
Missing dynamic instability by omitting flexion-extension views
Overlooking a pars stress injury in a young athlete with extension-related back pain
Attributing all symptoms to the slip without excluding coexisting stenosis or disc pathology
management: Conservative management for most low-grade slips with activity modification, physiotherapy focused on core stabilisation, and analgesia
Analgesia with NSAIDs and simple analgesics, with epidural or nerve-root corticosteroid injection for radicular symptoms
Bracing and activity restriction in young patients with an active pars lesion, monitoring growing patients for slip progression
Surgical decompression and instrumented fusion for high-grade slips, progressive slippage, or neurological compromise unresponsive to conservative care
Serial standing and flexion-extension radiographs to monitor slip grade and dynamic instability
Referral to spinal surgery for red-flag neurology, cauda equina features or refractory symptoms
